c00-p02: I ask the children to forgive me for dedicating this book to a grown-up. I have a serious excuse: this grown-up is the best friend I have in the world. I have another excuse: this grown-up can understand everything, even books for children. I have a third excuse: this grown-up lives in France, where he is hungry and cold. He badly needs to be comforted. If all these excuses are not enough, then I will gladly dedicate this book to the child this grown-up once was. All grown-ups were children first. (But few of them remember it.) So I correct my dedication:
c00-p03:
TO LÉON WERTH
WHEN HE WAS A LITTLE BOY
c01-p01: When I was six years old I saw, once, a magnificent picture in a book about the virgin forest called "True Stories." It showed a boa constrictor swallowing a wild beast. Here is a copy of the drawing.
c01-p02: The book said: "Boa constrictors swallow their prey whole, without chewing it. After that they cannot move, and they sleep through the six months of their digestion."
c01-p03: I thought a great deal, then, about the adventures of the jungle, and in my turn I managed, with a coloured pencil, to make my first drawing. My Drawing Number One. It looked like this:
c01-p04: I showed my masterpiece to the grown-ups and asked them whether my drawing frightened them.
c01-p05: They answered: "Why should anyone be frightened by a hat?"
c01-p06: My drawing was not a picture of a hat. It was a picture of a boa constrictor digesting an elephant. So I drew the inside of the boa constrictor, so that the grown-ups could understand. They always need things explained. My Drawing Number Two looked like this:
c01-p07: The grown-ups advised me to put aside my drawings of boa constrictors, from the outside or the inside, and to take an interest instead in geography, history, arithmetic and grammar. That is how, at the age of six, I gave up a magnificent career as a painter. I had been discouraged by the failure of my Drawing Number One and my Drawing Number Two. Grown-ups never understand anything by themselves, and it is tiring for children to have to explain things to them, always and always.
c01-p08: So I had to choose another profession, and I learned to fly aeroplanes. I have flown a little over all parts of the world. And geography, it is true, has been very useful to me. At a glance I could tell China from Arizona. That is very handy if you get lost in the night.
c01-p09: In the course of my life I have had heaps of dealings with heaps of serious people. I have lived a great deal among grown-ups. I have seen them up close. It has not much improved my opinion of them.
c01-p10: Whenever I met one who seemed to me a little clear-sighted, I tried the experiment of showing him my Drawing Number One, which I have always kept. I wanted to find out whether he was truly a person of understanding. But always the answer came back: "That is a hat." Then I would not talk to him about boa constrictors, or virgin forests, or stars. I would bring myself down to his level. I would talk to him about bridge, and golf, and politics, and neckties. And the grown-up would be very pleased to have met such a sensible man.
c02-p01: So I lived alone, with no one I could really talk to, until I had a breakdown in the Sahara Desert, six years ago. Something had broken in my engine. And since I had with me neither a mechanic nor any passengers, I got ready to attempt, all alone, a difficult repair. For me it was a question of life or death. I had barely enough water to drink for eight days.
c02-p02: So the first night I fell asleep on the sand, a thousand miles from any inhabited land. I was far more isolated than a shipwrecked sailor on a raft in the middle of the ocean. So you can imagine my surprise when, at daybreak, I was woken by an odd little voice. It said:
c02-p06: I jumped to my feet as if I had been struck by lightning. I rubbed my eyes hard. I looked hard. And I saw a most extraordinary little fellow, who was studying me gravely. Here is the best portrait that, later on, I managed to make of him. But my drawing, of course, is far less charming than its model. That is not my fault. I had been discouraged in my career as a painter by the grown-ups, at the age of six, and I had never learned to draw anything except boa constrictors from the outside and boa constrictors from the inside.
c02-p07: So I stared at this apparition with eyes round with astonishment. Do not forget that I was a thousand miles from any inhabited region. And yet my little fellow seemed to be neither lost, nor dying of exhaustion, nor dying of hunger, nor dying of thirst, nor dying of fear. He did not look at all like a child lost in the middle of the desert, a thousand miles from any inhabited region. When at last I managed to speak, I said to him:
c02-p09: And he repeated, very softly, as if it were a matter of great seriousness:
c02-p11: When a mystery is too overwhelming, one does not dare to disobey. Absurd as it seemed to me, a thousand miles from any inhabited place and in danger of death, I took a sheet of paper and a fountain pen out of my pocket. But then I remembered that I had mostly studied geography, history, arithmetic and grammar, and I told the little fellow (a little crossly) that I did not know how to draw. He answered:
c02-p12: "That doesn't matter. Draw me a sheep."
c02-p13: Since I had never drawn a sheep, I drew for him one of the only two drawings I was capable of. The one of the boa constrictor from the outside. And I was astounded to hear the little fellow answer:
c02-p14: "No! No! I don't want an elephant inside a boa constrictor. A boa constrictor is very dangerous, and an elephant takes up far too much room. Where I live, everything is very small. I need a sheep. Draw me a sheep."
c02-p16: He looked at it closely, and then:
c02-p17: "No! That one is already very sick. Make me another."
c02-p20: "You can see for yourself... that isn't a sheep, that's a ram. It has horns..."
c02-p21: So I did my drawing over once more. But it was rejected, like the others:
c02-p22: "That one is too old. I want a sheep that will live a long time."
c02-p23: By then I had run out of patience, since I was in a hurry to start taking my engine apart, so I scribbled this drawing.
c02-p25: "This is the box. The sheep you want is inside."
c02-p26: But I was very surprised to see my young judge's face light up:
c02-p27: "That is exactly the way I wanted it! Do you think this sheep will need a great deal of grass?"
c02-p29: "Because where I live everything is very small..."
c02-p30: "There will surely be enough. I have given you a very small sheep."
c02-p31: He bent his head over the drawing:
c02-p32: "Not so small as all that... Look! He has gone to sleep..."
c02-p33: And that is how I made the acquaintance of the little prince.
c03-p01: It took me a long time to understand where he came from. The little prince, who asked me a great many questions, never seemed to hear mine. It was words spoken by chance that, little by little, revealed everything to me. So, when he first caught sight of my aeroplane (I shall not draw my aeroplane; that drawing is much too complicated for me), he asked me:
c03-p03: "It is not a thing. It flies. It is an aeroplane. It is my aeroplane."
c03-p04: And I was proud to let him know that I could fly. Then he cried out:
c03-p05: "What! You fell out of the sky!"
c03-p08: And the little prince broke into a very pretty peal of laughter, which annoyed me very much. I like my misfortunes to be taken seriously. Then he added:
c03-p09: "So you come from the sky too! Which planet are you from?"
c03-p10: At once I caught a glimmer of light in the mystery of his presence, and I asked abruptly:
c03-p12: But he did not answer. He was shaking his head gently, all the while looking at my aeroplane:
c03-p13: "It's true that on that, you can't have come from very far away..."
c03-p14: And he sank into a reverie that lasted a long time. Then, taking my sheep out of his pocket, he became absorbed in the contemplation of his treasure.
c03-p15: You can imagine how intrigued I was by this half-confidence about "the other planets." So I did my best to find out more:
c03-p16: "Where do you come from, my little fellow? Where is this 'where I live'? Where do you want to take my sheep?"
c03-p17: After a thoughtful silence he answered:
c03-p18: "The good thing about the box you have given me is that at night he can use it as his house."
c03-p19: "Of course. And if you are good, I will give you a rope as well, to tie him up during the day. And a stake."
c03-p20: The suggestion seemed to shock the little prince:
c03-p21: "Tie him up? What a funny idea!"
c03-p22: "But if you don't tie him up, he will wander off anywhere, and he will get lost..."
c03-p23: And my friend burst out laughing again:
c03-p24: "But where do you think he would go!"
c03-p26: Then the little prince remarked gravely:
c03-p27: "That doesn't matter, it's so small where I live!"
c03-p28: And, with a little melancholy, perhaps, he added:
c03-p29: "Straight ahead of you, you can't go very far..."
c04-p01: So I had learned a second very important thing: that the planet he came from was hardly any bigger than a house!
c04-p02: That could not surprise me much. I knew very well that apart from the big planets like the Earth, Jupiter, Mars and Venus, which have been given names, there are hundreds of others that are sometimes so small that one has great trouble seeing them through a telescope. When an astronomer discovers one of them, he gives it a number for a name. He calls it, for example, "Asteroid 3251."
c04-p03: I have serious reasons to believe that the planet the little prince came from is Asteroid B 612.
c04-p04: This asteroid has been seen only once through a telescope, in 1909, by a Turkish astronomer.
c04-p05: He had then made a grand presentation of his discovery at an International Congress of Astronomy.
c04-p06: But nobody had believed him because of the way he was dressed. Grown-ups are like that.
c04-p07: Fortunately for the reputation of Asteroid B 612, a Turkish dictator ordered his people, on pain of death, to dress in the European fashion. The astronomer gave his presentation again in 1920, in a very elegant suit. And this time everybody agreed with him.
c04-p08: If I have told you these details about Asteroid B 612, and if I have trusted you with its number, it is because of the grown-ups. Grown-ups love figures. When you tell them about a new friend, they never ask you about what really matters. They never say to you: "What does his voice sound like? What games does he like best? Does he collect butterflies?" Instead they ask: "How old is he? How many brothers has he? How much does he weigh? How much money does his father make?" Only then do they think they know him. If you say to the grown-ups: "I saw a beautiful house made of pink bricks, with geraniums in the windows and doves on the roof..." they cannot picture that house at all. You have to say to them: "I saw a house worth a hundred thousand francs." Then they cry out: "How pretty it is!"
c04-p09: So if you say to them: "The proof that the little prince existed is that he was charming, that he laughed, and that he wanted a sheep. When someone wants a sheep, that is proof that he exists," they will shrug their shoulders and treat you like a child! But if you tell them: "The planet he came from is Asteroid B 612," then they will be convinced, and they will leave you in peace with their questions. They are like that. One must not hold it against them. Children should be very forgiving towards grown-ups.
c04-p10: But of course, we who understand life couldn't care less about numbers! I would have liked to begin this story the way fairy tales begin. I would have liked to say:
c04-p11: "Once upon a time there was a little prince who lived on a planet hardly any bigger than himself, and who needed a friend..." To those who understand life, that would have seemed far more true.
c04-p12: For I do not want my book to be read lightly. It gives me so much sorrow to tell these memories. It is already six years since my friend went away with his sheep. If I try to describe him here, it is so that I will not forget him. It is sad to forget a friend. Not everyone has had a friend. And I could become like the grown-ups, who are no longer interested in anything but figures. That is another reason why I bought a box of paints and some pencils. It is hard to take up drawing again at my age, when one has never made any attempt except a boa constrictor from the outside and a boa constrictor from the inside, at the age of six! I shall try, of course, to make my portraits as true to life as I can. But I am not at all sure I shall succeed. One drawing works, and the next one no longer looks like him. I make mistakes about his size, too. Here the little prince is too tall. There he is too small. I am unsure, too, about the colour of his clothes. So I fumble along, this way and that, as best I can. In the end I shall make mistakes about certain more important details as well. But that, you will have to forgive me. My friend never explained anything. Perhaps he thought I was like him. But I, unfortunately, do not know how to see sheep through the sides of boxes. Perhaps I am a little like the grown-ups. I must have grown old.
